title: Layer-Controlled Intermolecular Coupling and Many-Body Effects in C$_{60}$ Films
authors: Hai-Lan Luo, Weitang Li, Luca Moreschini, Jonathan Denlinger, Zhigang Shuai, Claudia Ojeda-Aristizabal, Alessandra Lanzara
abstract: Crystalline C$_{60}$ is a molecular solid whose electronic properties emerge from the interplay of intermolecular hopping, electron correlations, and electron-vibration coupling. Unlike moir$\rm\acute{e}$ van der Waals heterostructures, where interaction strength is commonly tuned by twist angle, molecular materials offer a complementary route in which layer number, molecular orientation, and substrate registry provide experimentally accessible control parameters. Here we present a systematic thickness-dependent angle-resolved photoemission study of C$_{60}$ films, spanning the monolayer to the bulk limit. The HOMO-derived band exhibits a non-monotonic evolution: the intermediate-thickness film shows larger bandwidth, reduced effective mass, and pronounced gap-like and sub-band features. The experimental trends, together with Holstein-model simulations, point to strengthened effective intermolecular electronic coupling and enhanced electron-phonon-induced spectral renormalization in the intermediate-thickness regime. These results identify a dimensional crossover in C$_{60}$ films and establish layer number as an effective knob for engineering electronic structure and many-body interactions in molecular thin films.
summary: This work investigates how controlling the thickness of C60 molecular films tunes their electronic properties by manipulating intermolecular coupling and electron-phonon interactions. Using ARPES and Holstein model simulations, the authors demonstrate a non-monotonic evolution, identifying an optimal intermediate thickness where coupling effects are maximized. This establishes layer number as a powerful, experimentally accessible knob for engineering correlated electronic states in molecular thin films.
main_problem: To systematically understand how dimensionality (layer number) controls the electronic structure and many-body interactions in crystalline C60 films.
main_result: The intermediate-thickness film regime shows the largest bandwidth and minimum effective mass, indicating strengthened effective intermolecular electronic coupling and enhanced electron-phonon renormalization.
method: The study combines Angle-Resolved Photoemission Spectroscopy (ARPES) experiments with theoretical modeling using the Holstein Hamiltonian.
model_or_system: The physical system is crystalline C60 molecular films grown on a Bi2Se3 substrate. The electronic properties are governed by intermolecular hopping, electron correlations, and electron-vibration coupling.
key_observables: HOMO-derived band bandwidth (W), effective mass (m*), gap-like features, and sub-band formation.
important_parameters: Film thickness (layer number), electron-phonon coupling strength (reorganization energy).
main_assumptions: The Holstein model provides a minimal phenomenological description of the electron-phonon interaction, and the HOMO bandwidth is defined as the energy range of the dominant spectral envelope.
figures_summary: Figures show thickness-dependent ARPES band structures, quantitative analysis of W and m* vs. thickness, and simulated spectral functions from the Holstein model comparing weak, intermediate, and strong coupling regimes.
paper_structure: The paper systematically presents experimental ARPES data showing thickness dependence, correlates these trends with theoretical predictions from the Holstein model, and uses the model to pinpoint the physical origin (electron-phonon coupling) of spectral features in the intermediate thickness regime.
why_interesting: The interplay between structural control (layer number) and emergent many-body physics (electron-phonon coupling) in molecular solids is highly relevant to understanding correlated phenomena in low-dimensional quantum materials.
